title: SST Martinotti Cells
intro: Somatostatin-expressing Martinotti cells sit in layers 2/3 and 5 and send their axons up to layer 1, where they inhibit the apical tufts of pyramidal cells. They are the cortex's dendritic inhibitors: rather than deciding when a cell fires, they decide which of its inputs count, in particular the top-down and contextual inputs that arrive on the tuft. They are recruited slowly, by sustained activity, through facilitating synapses.

items: Morphology: first described by Carlo Martinotti in 1889. Bitufted or multipolar dendrites, and an ascending axon that branches widely in layer 1, often across several columns. Non-Martinotti SST cells in layer 4 target layer 4 instead, and inhibit PV cells there (Xu et al. 2013).
Firing: low-threshold spiking (LTS) and adapting; many show rebound bursts after hyperpolarisation from a T-type calcium current. Higher input resistance and slower membrane than PV cells.

Inputs: excitation from local pyramidal cells through strongly facilitating synapses. A single pyramidal spike barely affects them, but a burst or sustained train recruits them strongly (Silberberg & Markram 2007; Kapfer et al. 2007). VIP cells inhibit them; cholinergic input can excite them.
Outputs: GABA-A synapses on the distal dendrites and tufts of pyramidal cells, plus inhibition of PV and VIP cells. SST cells hardly inhibit each other (Pfeffer et al. 2013).
Electrical coupling: SST cells are coupled to one another by gap junctions, forming a second electrically coupled interneuron network separate from the PV network (Gibson, Beierlein & Connors 1999).

Gating dendritic integration: SST inhibition on the tuft blocks calcium spikes and NMDA plateaus, so it decides whether feedback can turn single spikes into bursts in layer 5 cells (Murayama et al. 2009 showed this in vivo).

Frequency-dependent disynaptic inhibition: because pyramidal-to-SST synapses facilitate, a pyramidal cell firing at high rate recruits SST inhibition onto its neighbours' dendrites after a delay of tens of milliseconds. This is a slow, activity-dependent form of lateral inhibition (Silberberg & Markram 2007).
Surround suppression: in mouse V1, SST cells summate over large regions of visual space and contribute to the suppression of responses to large stimuli (Adesnik et al. 2012).

Learning control: by controlling dendritic depolarisation, SST cells regulate where and when plasticity happens in pyramidal dendrites; motor learning reshapes SST activity in motor cortex (Chen et al. 2015).
Izhikevich (2003) low-threshold spiking preset: a = 0.02, b = 0.25, c = −65, d = 2. The b = 0.25 coupling gives rebound responses.
Pospischil et al. (2008): a minimal HH model of cortical LTS cells with a T-type calcium current, fitted to recordings.
Blue Brain's MC (Martinotti) m-types in layers 2 to 6 with cAD, bAC and bSTUT e-types.

Circuit models: Litwin-Kumar et al. (2016) and Garcia del Molino et al. (2017) analysed PV-SST-VIP networks and showed how top-down input to VIP can either raise or lower pyramidal activity depending on network state; Yang, Murray and Wang (2016) modelled SST-targeted dendritic inhibition as a mechanism for routing which pathway reaches the soma.

Facilitating synapses for SST recruitment are modelled with the Tsodyks-Markram short-term plasticity model, with a small initial release probability U (about 0.1) and a long facilitation time constant.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Add SST-like cells once your excitatory cells have an apical or distal compartment; SST inhibition belongs there, not on the soma.
Use facilitating synapses from excitatory cells onto SST cells; otherwise SST cells behave like a slower copy of PV cells and lose their role.
Do not connect SST cells to each other; connect them to PV and VIP cells.
SST-mediated inhibition is a natural mechanism for 'only accept a prediction when context allows', which fits HTM-style distal or apical segments.
